title: Injection and Input Attacks: Quick Revision Notes
summary: Revision notes on SQL injection, parameterized queries, ORM pitfalls, command injection, path traversal, SSRF and input validation, from the shared root cause to the fixes and a final cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Injection Mental Model
points: Injection = untrusted input crossing a trust boundary and being interpreted as code or commands by an interpreter (SQL engine, shell, filesystem, HTTP client)
Root cause is mixing the data channel and the code channel in one string; the fix is to keep them separate, not to clean the string
Source to sink: user input (query, header, cookie, JSON body, filename) flows to a dangerous sink (query exec, shell call, file open, outbound fetch)
Example: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + input + "'" with input ' OR '1'='1 returns every row
Interview Point: Why is escaping weaker than parameterization? What is a sink? Why is client-side validation not a defense?

chapters.title: SQL Injection and Parameterized Queries
points: Parameterized (prepared) query sends the SQL template and the values separately, so values can never change query structure
In-band (UNION, error-based) returns data in the response; blind (boolean, time-based) infers it from true/false or delays; out-of-band exfiltrates through DNS or HTTP
Safe: cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=%s", (uid,)) and JDBC PreparedStatement with ?; unsafe: f-string, concatenation or String.format into SQL
Placeholders bind values only, not table names, column names or ORDER BY direction; allowlist those identifiers in code instead
Interview Point: How do prepared statements stop injection? Can you parameterize a table name? What is blind SQLi? Why does least-privilege DB access limit the damage?

chapters.title: ORM Pitfalls and Command Injection
points: ORMs parameterize by default but raw escape hatches reopen injection: Django .raw() and .extra(), SQLAlchemy text(f"..."), Sequelize.query with interpolation, Rails where("name='#{x}'")
Safe ORM raw use passes bind params: text("... WHERE id=:id"), {"id": uid}; the risk is the string you build, not the library
Mass assignment and operator injection: passing a request body straight into a filter lets an attacker send {"$ne": null} (NoSQL) or set is_admin=true
Command injection: user input reaching a shell lets ; | && $() backticks run extra commands, e.g. ping 8.8.8.8; rm -rf /
Fix: avoid the shell, use argument arrays (subprocess.run(["ping","-c","1",host]), shell=False); shell=True or os.system with input is the bug; allowlist and validate arguments too
Interview Point: Does using an ORM make you immune? Why is subprocess with a list safer than a shell string? What is operator injection in NoSQL?

chapters.title: Path Traversal, SSRF and Input Validation
points: Path traversal: ../ sequences (also encoded %2e%2e%2f, absolute paths, symlinks) escape the intended directory, e.g. /download?file=../../etc/passwd
Fix: resolve the full path (realpath) then check it starts with the base directory, or map IDs to filenames; blocking the string '../' alone is bypassable
SSRF: the server fetches a user-supplied URL, so attackers reach internal services and cloud metadata such as http://169.254.169.254/ to steal instance credentials

SSRF defenses: allowlist hosts, resolve DNS and block private/loopback/link-local IPs, re-validate every redirect target (stops 302-to-internal bypasses), pin the validated IP for the connection (stops DNS rebinding), disable unneeded schemes (file://, gopher://), use IMDSv2 on AWS

Input validation: allowlist (type, length, format, range) beats blocklist; validate server-side, canonicalize before checking, and treat it as defense in depth, not a replacement for parameterization or output encoding
Interview Point: How do you stop path traversal after decoding? Why is SSRF dangerous in the cloud? Allowlist vs blocklist? Where should validation happen?

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
points: Mistake: relying on escaping or a manual quote-stripping function instead of parameters; fix: bind parameters everywhere
Mistake: parameterizing values but concatenating ORDER BY, table or column names from input; fix: map input to a fixed allowlist of identifiers
Mistake: validating only on the client or only before decoding; fix: server-side validation after canonicalization
Mistake: running the app with a DB account that can DROP or read all schemas; fix: least-privilege accounts and read-only users where possible, plus generic error messages with no SQL or stack traces
Interview Point: Name three injection defenses in order of strength. How would you review code for injection? What logs or tests (SAST, DAST, fuzzing) catch these?

chapters.title: Injection Defenses Cheat Sheet
points: Table: attack, sink, primary fix: SQLi to query exec, bind parameters; command injection to shell, argument array with shell=False; path traversal to file open, realpath plus base-dir check; SSRF to outbound fetch, host allowlist plus private-IP block
Safe vs unsafe snippets: execute(sql, params) vs f"...{x}"; subprocess.run([...]) vs os.system(cmd)
Payload recognizers: ' OR 1=1--, ; id, ../../etc/passwd, http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
Layers in order: parameterize or avoid the interpreter, allowlist validation, least privilege, safe error handling, monitoring
Interview Point: Summarize the single rule behind all of these (never let data become code) and give one example per attack
